hints: Focus on what alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet actually describe - the local coiling or folding of a short section of polypeptide chain held by hydrogen bonds, not the amino acid sequence or the whole 3D molecule.
walkthrough:
Link Helix and Sheet to a Structural Level**
You are told alpha-keratin consists of many alpha-helices and beta-keratin of many beta-pleated sheets. Both of these are classic examples of the way a polypeptide chain is locally folded and held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of the backbone. In syllabus terms that is the secondary structure, distinct from primary (sequence), tertiary (overall 3D folding of one polypeptide) and quaternary (association of more than one polypeptide).

hints: Think about what is identical in every protein that a protease attacks - what type of bond is always hydrolysed, even if the R-groups around it differ?
walkthrough:
Remember What a Protease Actually Breaks**
A common slip is to think an enzyme must be totally specific to one whole protein. A protease hydrolyses peptide bonds, and every protein contains peptide bonds. If the amino acids around the bond are the same or similar, the same active site can bind and break them.

Apply Active Site Fit**
Binding still depends on shape. Different proteins can have a similar local shape that is complementary to the protease active site, or the active site has enough flexibility to accommodate similar substrates. That is why one protease can act on more than one type of protein.

Final answer: The region hydrolysed between the same amino acids / all substrates contain peptide bonds; or substrates have similar shape so fit the same active site with complementary shape / active site has some flexibility.

hints: Start from the stem clue - keratin has a high proportion of cysteine with sulfur-containing R groups. What strong covalent bond forms between two cysteines?
Think about the general fibrous protein model - soluble or insoluble, globular or long fibres, loosely or tightly packed, and how that would keep water and enzymes out.
To get three marks, list several different stabilising features - other bonds between chains besides the sulfur bond, and how close packing helps.
walkthrough:
Use the Cysteine Clue**
You are told keratin is rich in cysteine which has sulfur in its R group. Two cysteines on adjacent chains form disulfide bridges, which are strong covalent bonds. A high proportion of these cross-links makes filaments very resistant to unfolding and to protease attack.

Add the Fibrous Protein Model**
Keratin is fibrous, not globular. Fibrous proteins are insoluble in water, with long chains tightly and closely packed together. That packing excludes water and hides peptide bonds inside so keratinase cannot easily reach them.

Build Up Other Interactions**
Stability is not only disulfides. Many hydrogen bonds between polypeptides and many hydrophobic interactions between hydrophobic R groups add further strength. Together insolubility + disulfides + hydrogen bonds + hydrophobic interactions + tight packing explain why feathers are not easily degraded.

Final answer: Any three from: fibrous protein; insoluble / does not dissolve easily; many disulfide bridges / covalent bonds due to cysteines; many hydrogen bonds between polypeptides; many hydrophobic interactions; tight / close packing of chains / polypeptides; peptide bonds not accessible to enzyme.

walkthrough:
Read Temperature Ranges from Fig. 2.1 at 60%**
Put a ruler at 60% on the y-axis. K12 (filled dot) crosses at about 41 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ on the way up and about 63 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ on the way down. A22 (x) crosses at about 36 to 36.5 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ and about 57 $^{\circ}\text{C}$. P3 (open circle) crosses at about 29 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ and about 56 $^{\circ}\text{C}$. Those intervals are already partly given in Table 2.1 to help you check.

Read pH Ranges from Fig. 2.2 at 60%**
Do the same on the pH graph. K12 crosses at about pH 6.8 to 6.9 and pH 8.4. A22 crosses at pH 6.0 and pH 9.0. P3 crosses at about pH 5.3 and pH 7.5. Quote pH with no units and temperature in $^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Compare Spans to Find Widest**
Calculate span: temperature spans are K12 about 22 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, A22 about 20.5 to 21 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, P3 about 27 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, so P3 has the widest working range of temperature. pH spans are K12 about 1.5 to 1.6, A22 3.0, P3 2.2, so A22 has the widest working range of pH. This fits the idea that an industrial feather-degrading enzyme must tolerate varying conditions.

Final answer: K12 temperature 41-63 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, pH 6.8/6.9-8.4; A22 temperature 36/36.5-57 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, pH 6.0-9.0; P3 temperature 29-56 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, pH 5.3-7.5. Widest temperature range: P3; widest pH range: A22.

walkthrough:
Set the Detergent Context**
Detergent proteases need high relative activity in alkaline conditions and useful activity at wash temperatures. You must quote evidence from both graphs with correct units: temperature in $^{\circ}\text{C}$, pH, and relative activity in %. Using only one figure limits marks.

Pick Out Advantages with Data**
From Fig. 2.2, both enzymes suit alkaline washes. A22 shows greatest activity at pH 7.5 to 8.0 and at least 60% activity from pH 7.5 to 9.0; K12 is active between pH 7.5 to 8.0/8.5 with optimum near pH 8.0. From Fig. 2.1, both work over a wide temperature span - about 21 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ for A22 and 22 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ for K12 - with good, above 60%, activity at medium to hotter washes, and K12 retains about 37 to 43% activity even at 20 to 30 $^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Balance with Disadvantages and Wash Meaning**
From Fig. 2.1, activity is low at extremes: for A22 poor stain removal at 30 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 70 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 80 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, for K12 at 20 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 30 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 70 $^{\circ}\text{C}$. From Fig. 2.2, activity falls at higher pH above about pH 9.0. Link to washes: some low-temperature activity saves energy for heating water, higher-temperature activity helps sanitise and remove stains faster, K12 is more thermostable with higher optimum temperature but costs more energy, while A22 tolerates a wider alkaline pH range.

Final answer: Must include pH and $^{\circ}\text{C}$ and % at least once, using both figures. e.g. Advantage temperature: A22 and K12 active over wide range, e.g. 20.5/21 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ span for A22, 22 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ span for K12, with good activity at medium/hotter washes; K12 active at low temperature. Disadvantage temperature: low activity at 30 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 70 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 80 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ for A22 or 20 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 30 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ / 70 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ for K12. Advantage pH: active in alkaline conditions, e.g. A22 greatest at pH 7.5-8.0 / at least 60% pH 7.5-9.0, K12 active pH 7.5-8.0/8.5, optimum pH 8.0. Disadvantage pH: decrease at higher pH. Linked wash point e.g. some low temperature activity saves energy, high temperature sanitises, K12 more thermostable, A22 wider pH tolerance.
